questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male with a chronic history of diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolemia came to the clinic for follow-up. His BP has not been under control for many years. He has a vascular lesion similar to the image shown below. What does this image indicate? {{caption_text}}

options.label: B
options.text: Thick arterial wall due to deposition of pink, hyaline material

options.label: D
options.text: Lipid deposition within the vessel wall

questions.solutionHtml:
of uncontrolled hypertension shows an onion-skin appearance. Usually seen in malignant hypertension.

There are 2 types of hypertension:

  • Benign HTN: Hyaline arteriosclerosis
  • Malignant HTN: Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis

Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis:

  • It is characterized by concentric thickening of the arteriolar walls due to smooth muscle hyperplasia.
  • Because of long-term HTN and sudden spikes in blood pressure, proliferation of smooth muscles and fibroblasts occurs.
    • This results in the narrowing of the lumen and onion skin appearance.
  • Seen in Malignant Hypertension

Thick arterial wall due to deposition of pink, hyaline material (Option B): Hyaline arteriosclerosis is characterized by the thickening of arterial walls caused by the deposition of a pink hyaline substance due to leakage of plasma proteins through damaged endothelial cells.

  • Seen in benign hypertension and diabetes mellitus.

 





Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Pages 492, 493.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male presents with high pulse pressure. Histopathological examination is shown below. The arteries appear thickened, but there is no significant luminal narrowing. Which of the following conditions is the likely cause? {{caption_text}}
questions.solutionHtml:
n:
  • Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis, also known as calcific medial degeneration:
    • Calcific: Blue coloured dystrophic calcification due to old age.
    • Medial: Calcium is getting deposited into the tunica media of the blood vessel.
    • Degeneration: Degeneration occurring due to old age and not due to any pathology.
  • It is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally in imaging studies such as X-rays or histopathological examinations.

Atherosclerosis (Option A): Due to hypercholesterolemia, and on HPE foam cells are seen in blood vessels.

Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis (Option C): Seen in malignant hypertension.

Hyaline arteriosclerosis (Option D): Seen in benign hypertension and diabetes.

 





Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Pages 492, 493.

questions.stem: Arrange the following steps of atherosclerosis formation in the correct order. Endothelial injury and dysfunction Accumulation of lipoproteins Platelet adhesion and factor release Smooth muscle and collagen formation
questions.solutionHtml:
>Atherosclerosis is the thickening or hardening of the arteries caused by a buildup of plaque in the inner lining of an artery.
  • It is the arterial wall's chronic inflammatory and healing response to endothelial injury.

    •  

    Risk factors:

    Nonmodifiable (Constitutional)

    • Genetic abnormalities
    • Family history
    • Increasing age
    • Male gender

    Modifiable

    • Hyperlipidemia
    • Hypertension
    • Cigarette smoking
    • Diabetes
    • Inflammation
    • Hyperhomocysteinemia
    • Metabolic syndrome

     

    The pathogenesis of atherosclerosis is as follows:

    1. Endothelial injury and dysfunction cause increased vascular permeability, leukocyte adhesion, and thrombosis.
    2. Accumulation of lipoproteins (LDL)
    3. Monocyte adhesion to the endothelium, migration into intima and transformation into macrophages and foam cells.
    4. Platelet adhesion.
    5. Factor release from activated platelets, macrophages inducing SMC(smooth muscle cell) recruitment
    6. SMC proliferation, extracellular matrix production(ECM)
    7. Lipid accumulation is both extracellular and within macrophages and SMC.
    8. Calcification of ECM and necrotic debris.

     




    Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Pages 493-498

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain radiating to his back. On physical examination, a pulsatile mass is palpated in his abdomen. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and smoking. Based on the clinical presentation and risk factors, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
:
  • The clinical presentation of sudden-onset severe abdominal pain radiating to the back, along with a pulsatile abdominal mass, is highly suggestive of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).
  • The primary cause of aneurysms is atherosclerosis, with other factors including genetic predisposition, connective tissue disorders: Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, trauma, and infection: Mycotic aneurysms.

Pathogenesis:

  • Aneurysms result from medial degeneration due to chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and atherosclerosis.
  • This process weakens the arterial wall, particularly in the abdominal aorta, leading to dilation and aneurysm formation.

Clinical Features:

  • Asymptomatic cases may be incidentally discovered during imaging studies.
  • Sudden-onset severe abdominal or back pain
  • Pulsatile abdominal mass on physical examination,
  • Hypotension or shock due to rupture in severe cases.

Management: Depending on the aneurysm size, symptoms, and patient’s condition.

  • Small asymptomatic AAAs (<5.5 cm)-Monitoring with periodic imaging
  • Symptomatic, rapidly expanding (>1 cm/year), or large (>5.5 cm) AAAs- Elective repair via open or endovascular procedure
  • Medical management- Slow atherosclerosis progression and reduce aneurysm risk.


Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Pages 504-507.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an intermediate-grade vascular tumour?
questions.solutionHtml:
cation of  vascular tumours:
  • Benign vascular tumour: Hemangioma, pyogenic granuloma, etc.
  • Intermediate vascular tumour: Kaposi sarcoma
  • Malignant vascular tumour: Angiosarcoma, hemangiopericytoma

Kaposi sarcoma is an intermediate-grade vascular tumour.

  • It is caused by Human Herpes Virus 8. (HHV8)
  • It is associated with HIV/Immunodeficiency.
  • M/c location is skin of lower limbs > lymph nodes

 



Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page 518.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the clinic with a rapidly expanding, clearly defined, bright red lesion on the face. Upon examination, the lesion feels soft, yields to pressure, and temporarily loses color when pressure is applied. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
ong>

Explanation:

The given clinical scenario suggests infantile/capillary hemangioma.

  • Capillary hemangiomas or infantile hemangiomas are frequently encountered in benign vascular growth in infants.
  • While most capillary hemangiomas are isolated, they can also occur as part of syndromes such as PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects, eye abnormalities, and sternal clefting).
  • They typically present as swiftly enlarging, vivid red lesions. A key distinguishing trait is their soft, yielding texture, which momentarily loses colour under pressure due to their abundant blood supply.
  • They follow a pattern of rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression.



Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Pages 519, 520.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient presents with a history of multiple tumours in various organs, including the brain, retina, and kidneys. On examination, retinal angiomas and cerebellar hemangioblastomas are noted. The patient's family history reveals similar manifestations in relatives. Which of the following lesions is commonly associated with this syndrome?
questions.solutionHtml:
he clinical scenario represents von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, commonly associated with cavernous hemangiomas.
  • VHL Syndrome is associated with the deletion of chromosome 3p.
  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
  • It is associated with Cavernous hemangiomas.

 




Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page 520.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old individual complains of a throbbing mass on the tip of their index finger. Upon examination, the lesion is bluish and extremely tender to the touch. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
g>Explanation:
  • Glomus tumours are benign tumours originating from the glomus bodies of blood vessels.-modified smooth muscle cells specialised in temperature regulation.
  • Glomus bodies: These are the arterio-venous (A-V) anastomoses responsible for thermoregulation of the body.
    • Usually present at the tip of fingers,
  • They typically manifest as excruciatingly painful, pulsating masses, often found under the nails of the fingers (subungual swelling).

 




Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page 520.

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman, 20 weeks pregnant, presents with a painful, growing, reddish lump on her gums (as shown below) that bleeds when brushing or eating. The lesion is tender, and she denies any history of trauma or irritation. What is the most likely diagnosis? {{caption_text}}
questions.solutionHtml:
"customMeta" data-dictid="89e3252d5b16927771833fb9b432ae">Capillary Hemangioma (also known as Pyogenic Granuloma or Granuloma Gravidarum or Pregnancy Tumor).

 

  • It regresses after pregnancy, so in most cases, surgical ressection or any treatment is not needed.
  • Microscopically: Lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH)




Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page 732.
